entities.name: Zumwalt-class destroyer
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Zumwalt-class destroyer, a class of stealthy guided missile destroyers, was initiated in the early 2000s and officially launched in 2013, representing a significant evolution in naval warfare technology for the United States Navy. Named after Admiral Elmo Zumwalt, the class is characterized by its distinctive angular design and advanced technologies, such as the Integrated Power System and the advanced radar and missile systems that enhance its combat capabilities. This class was a response to the changing dynamics of maritime security and the need for modern naval forces that could operate effectively in various combat scenarios across the globe.

The Zumwalt-class destroyer was primarily constructed at the Bath Iron Works in Maine, with the first ship, USS Zumwalt (DDG-1000), being commissioned on October 15, 2016. This class was designed to fulfill multi-mission roles, including land attack, anti-aircraft warfare, and anti-submarine warfare. With a displacement of 15,000 tons, it is one of the largest destroyers ever built for the U.S. Navy, capable of operating in both littoral zones and open ocean environments. The Zumwalt-class incorporates a stealthy profile to reduce radar cross-section and enhance survivability against modern threats, marking a significant advancement in naval architecture.

The legacy of the Zumwalt-class destroyer extends beyond its technological innovations; it symbolizes the U.S. Navy's shift towards a more versatile and technologically advanced fleet. Although production was limited to three ships, the design principles of the Zumwalt-class have influenced subsequent naval projects and discussions regarding future naval capabilities. The class has sparked debates within military and defense circles on the balance between cost, capability, and the evolving nature of maritime threats.
